```{r setup, include=FALSE}
site <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = site,
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
options(width = 100)
```

Most supported models need nothing special. The notes below cover the few
that do. Fits that `suest` can't use, such as penalized fits or models that
did not converge, stop with an error that explains why.

## Linear models

Linear models add an `lnvar` parameter (the log of the error variance) to the
combined coefficients and covariance matrix. It has no effect on predictions
or marginal effects.

## Linear panel models

For `plm::plm()` models, comparisons of slopes and changes are supported.
Confidence intervals and tests for average predicted levels at the
estimation-sample means are not: their standard errors can be missing or near
zero.

## Constant-dispersion negative binomial

- Stata's `nbreg, dispersion(constant)` is
  `glmmTMB(y ~ x, family = nbinom1())`, and `menbreg, dispersion(constant)`
  adds random effects, as in `glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | id), family = nbinom1())`.
  The conditional variance is `mu*(1 + exp(log_phi))`, and `log_phi` is
  Stata's `/lndelta`.
- Stata's default `nbreg` (mean dispersion) is `MASS::glm.nb()`, or
  `glmmTMB(family = nbinom2())` with random effects.

## Population-averaged (GEE) models

- `geeglm()` models can use independence, exchangeable, ar1, or unstructured
  working correlations. As in Stata, `suest` holds the working correlation
  at its estimate.
- geepack and Stata estimate unstructured correlations the same way, so
  their results match. They estimate ar1 correlations differently, so ar1
  coefficients and standard errors differ slightly. To reproduce R's ar1
  results in Stata, use `corr(fixed R)` (for example
  `xtlogit y x, pa corr(fixed R)`), where `R` has entries `alpha^|j - k|`
  and `alpha` is `model$geese$alpha`.
- For ar1, give `geeglm()` the time variable, `waves = time`, so the
  correlation depends on the time between observations; without it, geepack
  uses each observation's position in its panel. Stata leaves out panels
  whose times are unequally spaced unless you add `force`, which then uses
  the order of the observations.
- Unstructured correlations need each panel's waves to run 1, 2, ...; panels
  can end early but cannot skip a wave. geepack cannot fit unstructured
  correlations with skipped waves (R stops with a memory error), although
  Stata can.

## Parametric survival models

- Predictions from `survreg()` and `svysurvreg()` models of survival time
  (Weibull, exponential, lognormal, log-logistic) are median survival times,
  as after `streg`. `predict(type = "response")` instead gives
  exp(linear predictor), which is the median for lognormal and log-logistic
  models but not for Weibull and exponential ones.
- Stata's log likelihood after `streg` leaves out the sum of log times over
  the failures, so it is higher than survreg's and flexsurv's by that amount.
  Estimates and standard errors are the same.

## Gompertz and generalized gamma survival

- Stata's `streg, distribution(gompertz)` is
  `flexsurvreg(Surv(time, event) ~ x, dist = "gompertz")`, and
  `streg, distribution(ggamma)` is `dist = "gengamma"`. Stata's
  `ancillary()` and `anc2()` are flexsurv's `anc`, as in
  `anc = list(shape = ~ z)` for the Gompertz `gamma` or
  `anc = list(sigma = ~ z, Q = ~ z)` for the generalized gamma.
- Delayed entry, `stset time, failure(event) enter(time entry)`, is
  `Surv(entry, time, event)`.
- Predictions are median survival times, as after `streg`.
- flexsurv's optimizer can stop slightly short of the maximum, so estimates
  can differ from Stata's in the fourth or fifth decimal place (up to about
  1e-4 for a generalized gamma coefficient with flexsurv's default settings).

## Bivariate probit

- Stata's `biprobit (y1 = x z) (y2 = x w)` is
  `gjrm(list(y1 ~ x + z, y2 ~ x + w), margins = c("probit", "probit"),
  model = "B", data = d)`. Predictions are the probability that both
  outcomes equal 1, as after `biprobit`.
- GJRM approximates the bivariate normal probabilities closely but not
  exactly, so its estimates can differ from Stata's by about 1e-7.

## Generalized ordered models

- `VGAM::vglm()` with `cumulative(link = ..., reverse = TRUE)` is
  `gologit2` with the logit, probit, cloglog, or cauchit link
  (`"logitlink"`, `"probitlink"`, `"clogloglink"`, `"cauchitlink"`).
  `parallel = TRUE` is `gologit2, pl`, and `parallel = FALSE ~ x` frees `x`
  only, as in `gologit2, npl(x)`.
- gologit2's `link(loglog)` is `cumulative(link = "clogloglink",
  reverse = FALSE)`: the same model, with every coefficient's sign reversed.

## Zero-inflated models

When every model in the system is a `pscl::zeroinfl()` model (Poisson or
negative binomial), predictions and marginal effects take the same `type`
values as zeroinfl:

| `type` | Prediction | Stata `margins` after `zip` or `zinb` |
|---|---|---|
| `"response"` (the default) | Expected count | `predict(n)` |
| `"count"` | Mean of the count part | `expression(exp(predict(equation(depvar))))` |
| `"zero"` | Probability of a structural zero | `predict(pr)` |
| `"prob"` | `Pr(y = k)` for k = 0 to the largest observed count | `predict(pr(k))` |

Here `depvar` is the name of the count outcome, which names the count
equation. With `type = "prob"`, each count is a separate outcome, labeled
`model::0`, `model::1`, and so on. Negative-binomial probabilities depend on
the dispersion parameter, and their standard errors include its uncertainty.
Standard errors use the exact observed information, as Stata does.

```{r zeroinfl-types}
library(suest)
library(marginaleffects)
data("bioChemists", package = "pscl")

zip <- pscl::zeroinfl(art ~ fem + kid5 + ment | ment, data = bioChemists)
zinb <- pscl::zeroinfl(art ~ fem + kid5 + ment | ment, data = bioChemists,
                       dist = "negbin")
zi_fit <- suest(zip, zinb, model_names = c("ZIP", "ZINB"))

# Effect of mentor productivity on the probability of a structural zero,
# and its difference across the two models
avg_slopes(zi_fit, variables = "ment", type = "zero")
avg_slopes(zi_fit, variables = "ment", type = "zero", hypothesis = ~ pairwise)

# Predicted Pr(no articles) in each model
p <- avg_predictions(zi_fit, type = "prob")
p[p$group %in% c("ZIP::0", "ZINB::0"), ]
```

## Mixed models fitted with glmmTMB

- Predictions and marginal effects average over the random intercept, and
  over the random slope when there is one.
- Center continuous predictors and keep them in well-scaled units. glmmTMB's
  covariance matrix can be inaccurate with extreme predictor units even when
  the model reports convergence, and `suest` uses that covariance as supplied.
- For slopes of continuous predictors in logit random-slope models, use
  `numderiv = list("fdcenter", eps = 1e-4)` in `avg_slopes()` for more stable
  standard errors, and check that nearby step sizes (such as `5e-5` and
  `2e-4`) give similar answers.

## Several random slopes and three-level models

- `lmer()`, `glmer()`, `glmmTMB()`, and `clmm()` models can have several
  random slopes for the grouping variable, `(1 + x1 + x2 | school)`, and one
  level nested in it, `(1 + x1 | school) + (1 | school:class)` or
  `(1 | school/class)`. In Stata, these are
  `|| school: x1 x2, covariance(unstructured) || class:`. Independent terms,
  `(1 + x1 || school)`, and glmmTMB's `diag()` are Stata's
  `covariance(independent)`. Crossed random effects and a third grouping
  level are not supported.
- Slopes must be numeric data columns. Make a numeric 0/1 version of a
  factor, and create transformed variables (such as squares) before fitting.
- The variance parameters are each term's log standard deviations,
  `log_sd_school_x1`, and Fisher z correlations,
  `atanh_rho_school_intercept_x1`, as in Stata's `lns` and `atr`. A nested
  level is named with a dot: `log_sd_school.class_intercept`.
- Nonlinear models with these structures use the Laplace approximation (lme4
  allows adaptive quadrature only for a single random intercept), while
  suest2 requires adaptive quadrature. Stata's `me` commands with
  `intmethod(laplace)` give the same estimates and log likelihood, but the
  standard errors they report for these fits can differ from the exact
  Laplace standard errors by a few percent. Linear models agree with `mixed`
  exactly.
- Fits near a boundary, with a variance near zero or correlations near -1 or
  1, are refused even when lme4 does not flag them as singular. Simplify the
  random-effects structure.

## Survey models

- Binary probit and cloglog (`svyglm()`), ordered (`svyolr()`), multinomial,
  negative-binomial, and generalized ordered (`svy_vglm()`), and survival
  (`svysurvreg()`) models use exact observed information, as Stata does. Their
  standard errors can differ from the fitted model's own: `svyglm()` and VGAM
  use expected information, `svyolr()` uses a numerical Hessian, and for
  interval-censored outcomes survival's scale residuals are incorrect.
- These fits stop at fairly loose tolerances. For results that agree closely
  with Stata, tighten them: `control = list(reltol = 1e-12)` in `svyolr()` and
  `control = VGAM::vglm.control(criterion = "coefficients", epsilon = 1e-9)`
  in `svy_vglm()`.
- `svy_vglm()` multinomial models use the last category as the reference
  unless `multinomial(refLevel = )` says otherwise.
- `suest()` finds an `svyivreg()` model's design from its call, so keep that
  design object available.

## Stata models without an R version

For these Stata models, `suest` supports a model that answers the same
question. The last column fits the same model in Stata.

| Stata model | Use in R | Same model in Stata |
|---|---|---|
| `xtlogit, fe` | Random-intercept logit with each time-varying predictor's person mean added (`glmer()`, `glmmTMB()`, or `pglm()`); see [Within-person effects](within-person.html) | `xtlogit, re` or `melogit` with the person means |
| `xtmlogit, fe` | `nnet::multinom()` with the person means, clustered on person | `mlogit` with the person means, `vce(cluster id)` |
| `xtmlogit, re` | `nnet::multinom()` clustered on person | `mlogit, vce(cluster id)` |
| `xtnbreg, fe` | Fixed-effects Poisson, `fixest::fepois()` | `xtpoisson, fe` |
| `xtnbreg, re` | Random-intercept negative binomial, `glmmTMB()` | `menbreg` |
| `xtnbreg, pa` | Population-averaged Poisson, `geepack::geeglm()` | `xtpoisson, pa vce(robust)` |
| `mestreg` | `survreg()` clustered on the group | `streg, vce(cluster group)` |

Fixed-effects Poisson with robust standard errors is valid for overdispersed
counts, and `xtnbreg, fe` is not a true fixed-effects model (Allison and
Waterman 2002). The multinomial and survival stand-ins have no random effects,
so they estimate effects averaged over people rather than for a given person.

Allison, P. D., & Waterman, R. P. (2002). Fixed-effects negative binomial
regression models. *Sociological Methodology*, 32, 247-265.

## Models fitted with different packages

Models fitted by different packages can be combined, as long as they are
supported models.

```{r libraries}
library(suest)
library(marginaleffects)
```

`glm()` and `glm2::glm2()`:

```{r glm2-engine}
library(glm2)

dat <- mtcars
dat$am <- factor(dat$am)

standard <- glm(am ~ wt + hp, family = binomial("logit"), data = dat)
alternative <- glm2(am ~ wt + hp, family = binomial("logit"), data = dat)
engine_fit <- suest(standard, alternative, model_names = c("glm", "glm2"))
avg_comparisons(engine_fit, variables = "wt", newdata = dat)
```

`ordinal::clm()` and `MASS::polr()`. `clm()` models need flexible thresholds
and no scale or nominal-effects formula.

```{r clm-engine}
library(ordinal)

housing <- MASS::housing[rep(seq_len(nrow(MASS::housing)), MASS::housing$Freq),
                         c("Sat", "Infl", "Type", "Cont")]
rownames(housing) <- NULL
housing$Sat <- ordered(housing$Sat, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))

clm_model <- clm(Sat ~ Cont + Infl + Type, data = housing, link = "logit")
polr_model <- MASS::polr(Sat ~ Cont + Infl + Type, data = housing,
                         method = "logistic", Hess = TRUE)
ordinal_fit <- suest(clm_model, polr_model, model_names = c("clm", "polr"))
avg_comparisons(ordinal_fit, variables = "Cont", newdata = housing)
```
